Varuṇa's power is unfathomable. Neither the flying birds nor the flowing rivers can reach the boundary of his kingdom; they cannot exceed his power; they cannot restrain his anger (1-24-6). Neither sky nor rivers can reach the limit of Mitra and Varuṇa (1-151-9). Everything is contained in Varuṇa; the dwellings of all beings are in him (8-41 and 7 [as printed]); the three heavens and three earths are placed in him (7-87-5). Varuṇa is all-knowing. The flight of birds in the sky, the passing of ships on the sea, the course of the far-going wind — all of this is known to him; he sees all things that are past or to come (1-25-7, 9, 11); he is the witness of men's truth and falsehood (7-49-3). Creatures cannot even wink without him (2-28-6); the number of men's winkings is known to him; the deeds, plans and devices of every man are known to Varuṇa (Ath. Saṃ. 4-16-2 and 5). He can grasp everything in heaven and earth and whatever lies beyond them; however far one may run beyond the sky, no one can escape Varuṇa's sight (Ath. Saṃ. 4-16-4 and 5). That this omniscience is a personal quality of Varuṇa is shown by the fact that Agni is compared to him in this matter.  ==>  "Varuṇa's power is unfathomable. Savitṛ's is boundless brilliance. His golden light is without limit; it is unequalled by other deities (3-38-8; 7-38-1). He throws out this light, or scatters it. By this the sphere of the air, heaven and earth, the world, the cavities of the earth and the sky — all are lit up (1-35-7 and 8; 4-14-2; 4-53-4; 5-81-2). Raising his strong golden arms, which reach to the ends of the regions, he wakes all beings and blesses them (2-38-2; 4-53-3 and 4; 6-71-1 and 5; 7-45-2). Since other deities are compared to Savitṛ raising his arms, this too may be called a personal quality of his. Agni raises his arms like Savitṛ (1-95-7); Uṣas stretches out her light as Savitṛ stretches out his arms (7-39-2). Likewise Bṛhaspati too is prayed to, that the praise-words be uttered firmly (1-190-3). On the path that leads downward and upward, Savitṛ, seated in his golden chariot, goes looking at all beings (1-35-2 and 3). Before the time of dawn he sets out the chariot of the Aśvins (1-34-10). Following the path of the goddess Uṣas, he himself too shines (5-81-2). He has measured the regions of the earth; he goes to the three regions of heaven; he joins the rays of Sūrya (5-81-3 and 4). The word '*Sūryaraśmi*' occurs once in the Ṛgveda; it belongs to Savitṛ. Shining with Sūrya's rays, Savitṛ, of golden hair, ceaselessly throws his light from the eastern quarter (10-139-1). He goes three times around the sphere of the air, the three skies, and the three luminous regions of the upper world (4-53-5). The ancient paths that he follows in the sky are pure and easy to walk. Here his worshippers pray to him: '*Protect us*' (1-35-11). They pray: 'Join the life of the dead one to the place where living beings are' (10-17, 4 [as printed]). It is he who gives the gods immortality and men long life (4-54-2). It is he who gave immortality to the Ṛbhus who came to his house by the strength of their works (1-110-2 and 3). Savitṛ is prayed to as one prays to Sūrya, and also for the warding off of evil dreams (5-82-4)  ==>  "Savitṛ's is boundless brilliance. Let us now examine the history connected with him. Intoxicated by Soma-drinking, and accompanied by the Maruts, he makes himself ready for war with the Rākṣasa, the cause of drought, called Vṛtra, Ahi and so on. When he strikes Vṛtra with his vajra, heaven and earth tremble (1-80-11; 2-11-9 and 10; 6-17-9); even Tvaṣṭṛ, who made the vajra, trembles at the sight of Indra's wrath (10-80-14 [as printed]). With the vajra-weapon Indra smashes Vṛtra to bits (1-32-5; 1-61-10; 10-89-7); he strikes Vṛtra on the back with the vajra (1-32-7; 1-80-5), strikes him on the face with his own weapon (1-52-15). He finds and seizes the places without a guard (3-32-4; 5-32-5). He struck Vṛtra, who had enclosed the water (6-20-2, etc.), or the serpent that lay coiled around the water (4-19-2), he struck him; he defeated the serpent lying on the water (5-30-6); he killed the serpent who, enclosing the waters, shut out the sky (2-11-5) and split Vṛtra, who was covering the waters, as one splits a tree (2-14-2). In this context the epithet *apsujit* ('conqueror in the waters') is used of no other deity. 'Indra killed Vṛtra', 'he kills Vṛtra', 'kill Vṛtra' — such praises: taken all together, it is clear that this is an event taking place constantly. After the killing of Vṛtra Indra releases the waters in many dawns and autumn seasons (4-19-8), or is prayed to do so in the future (8-37-4). He splits the mountains so that waters flow, or so that cows come out (1-57-6; 10-89-7), and by the mere sound of the vajra this work is done (6-27-4). When the mountains were split, the streams burst out; the Rākṣasa was killed; like the udders of the mountains, the waters shut in all around came out (5-32-1 and 2). Having killed the Rākṣasa, broken the mountain into bits, burst open the well, he released the waters that had been shut up (1-57-6; 5-33-1). He sets free the streams that were like cows tied up (1-61-10), or they flow to the ocean like lowing cattle (1-32-2). Having won the cows and the Soma, he made the seven rivers flow (1-32-12; 2-12-12). The waters that had been bound (1-57-6; 1-103-2), the waters that had been seized by the serpent (2-11-2), he set free, he made channels for the streams with the vajra (2-15-3), made the water's stream flow to the ocean (2-19-3); he made flow the waters that had been blocked by Vṛtra (3-26-6; 4-17-1). but it is clear that it is not so important there. It is plainly said that Indra killed Vṛtra by his own power (1-165-8; 7-21-6; 10-138-6); yet, other deities are helpers to Indra in this work. The deities yoked Indra to the chariot for the sake of battle (1-55-3; 6-17-8) or for the killing of Vṛtra (8-12-22). To fight Vṛtra the deities increased his heroism (10-113-8), or gave him strength and ability (10-80-15 [as printed]; 6-20-2; 10-48-3; 10-120-3), or placed the vajra in his hand (2-20-8). Most of all it is the Maruts who urge him on and are friends to him (3-32-4; 10-73 [?]-1 and 2, etc.). When all the other deities fled in fear of Vṛtra (8-85-7; compare 4-18-11; Ai. Brā. 3-20), the Maruts stood by Indra; but in one place (8-7-31) it is said that the Maruts themselves once abandoned him. While he fought with Vṛtra, Agni, Soma and Viṣṇu too were helpers to him. The seers too stood by him in this war (5-30-8; 8-51-11; 10-44-9). The worshipper (*stotṛ*) placed the vajra in his hands (1-63-2), and the sacrifice was a help to the vajra in the killing of the Rākṣasa (3-32-12).
